articles.title: White House launches Trump TV following press bans
articles.summary: The White House on Monday launched Trump TV, a 24/7 stream on YouTube, days after President Trump banned reporters from CNN, Politico and MS NOW over their c...
articles.body:
The White House on Monday launched Trump TV, a 24/7 stream on YouTube, days after President Trump banned reporters from CNN, Politico and MS NOW over their coverage of him and his administration.

The inaugural video was a stream of Trump speaking at Mount Rushmore on July 3 as part of a livestream titled "Trump TV: The Essentials Station." The stream started at 7 p.m.

"Watch the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place," read the stream's description on YouTube. "Top videos, major remarks, and must-see highlights streaming 24/7 and updated in real time. Stay informed and stay up to date!"

The White House used a similar description on the social platform X but added, "Not every big moment has made it on your TV, now it can."

The video is also streamed via a YouTube window on the White House website . Beside the window is a box titled "White House Live." The window read that it was "Off Air" but advised viewers to "Stay Tuned." Below both windows is a chyron reading official updates and statements praising Trump's actions as president, among other texts.

It is unclear if Trump TV will play live events featuring the president and his administration.

A promo for Trump TV played on the White House's YouTube channel earlier in the day. The video used clips of characters from various shows and movies –– including "Seinfeld," "Family Guy," and "The Dark Knight" –– watching TV as the Buggles's "Video Killed the Radio Star" played in the background. The words "Trump TV" flashed across the screen over the clips.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) slammed Trump TV's rollout in the wake of his ban on White House reporters from CNN, Politico and MS NOW.

"First, Trump banned independent news from the White House," Newsom wrote on X . "Now, he's launching what is quite literally state-run TV to try drowning out the fact that he and his corrupt administration are failing the American people. This is truly autocratic behavior from a failed President."

Trump banned reporters from the three outlets on Friday as a result of what he claimed was "their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" He told reporters in the Oval Office that there was no particular reason for the timing of the ban and that it was "really just cumulative stories over the last two years."

All three outlets filed a lawsuit against the administration on Monday "to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," the outlets said in a joint statement.

Former White House Correspondents' Association President Weijia Jiang condemned the ban , noting in a Fox News interview that the U.S. does not have state-run media.

"An America cannot have state TV," Jiang said. "That's what makes America America … because you need independent actors to be able to be the observers. And if the government is only showing you what it wants, then you have to question: What are we missing?"

articles.title: Republicans were bullish about the Senate. Now they’re playing defense in red states.
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s economic agenda is becoming a particular problem in the Midwest.
articles.body:
Republicans are playing defense deep in their own territory as voter anger over price hikes puts more House and Senate seats in play in the midterms.

New rounds of big spending, visits from Trump administration officials and private conversations among top GOP officials overseeing the battle for control of Congress reveal a party rushing to shore up red seats and states President Donald Trump won handily in 2024.

In the House, the fight has expanded far outside the few-dozen seats considered the most competitive as Republicans start to unleash their massive warchest: Since Aug. 1, more than $110 million in ad bookings have gone toward Republican-held districts so red that Trump won them by double digits.

In the Senate, Republicans are racing to shore up Ohio GOP Sen. Jon Husted as the Midwest struggles under the weight of Trump's tariffs and high diesel prices. Trump and Vice President JD Vance are both expected to travel to the state before the midterms to boost Husted, according to four people familiar with the matter who were granted anonymity to discuss not-yet-public plans.

GOP leaders are also trying to keep a handle on contests in Iowa and Kansas — and they've quietly begun deprioritizing Georgia and even North Carolina, which a growing number of Republicans are privately bracing for Democrats to flip.

"We need to stop the contagion," said one senior GOP official, who, like others, was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the midterm landscape.

"The map is hilariously big right now," said one national Republican pollster.

Since Aug. 1, nearly two-thirds of advertising funds in House races have been booked or spent in races with GOP incumbents, according to a POLITICO analysis of data from AdImpact, which tracks political advertising.

That includes nearly $18 million to embattled Rep. Max Miller in Ohio's 7th District; $14.6 million to Texas' 15th District where Monica De La Cruz faces a challenge from Tejano Singer Bobby Pulido; $9.6 million in Alaska where Rep. Nick Begich faces a challenge from independent Bill Hill; and millions more to other districts that Trump carried by double digits two years ago.

The GOP holds a massive cash advantage over Democrats — which, for now, means they can afford to spend more broadly. Republican groups are dividing up the spending deluge in the final weeks ahead of the midterms, with Trump's MAGA Inc. affiliated super PAC spending heavily to shore up safer red seats and deter Democrats from pushing into those races.

"The voter enthusiasm [for Republican voters] is not where it needs to be but that's where a money advantage can make a really big impact," said Mark Bednar, a GOP strategist and former communications director for then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy.

Republicans have adjusted their Senate map expectations: They're still bullish about Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire. They're not as optimistic about North Carolina — which Trump won in 2024 — but they are hoping to force Democrats to spend more there.

Republicans are more concerned about Alaska and Texas. And their worries about Ohio have escalated amid soaring diesel prices and backlash to tariffs — challenges they're also confronting in Texas, Iowa, Michigan and Kansas .

Already two battleground candidates have called for ends to the Iran war, pointing to the high prices: Iowa GOP Senate nominee Ashley Hinson , whose team has grown increasingly wary of the tight race and Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers . Both Hinson and Rogers use top Trump pollster Tony Fabrizio to guide their campaigns.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment on Hinson's and Rogers' remarks.

Senior GOP operatives' own internal polling shows Trump's approval underwater in deep red states across the country. And an Iowa poll conducted last week by a Democratic-leaning pollster found Democrat Josh Turek with a one-point lead in the Senate race and Trump's approval at 43 percent in the state he won by more than 13 percentage points in 2024, according to a copy of the poll obtained by POLITICO.

"As more races come online, it very clearly is a defensive map for Republicans across the country," said a national GOP strategist working on multiple battleground races.

In Ohio, Republicans are optimistic that their attacks on former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown's voting record are starting to break through, based on recent internal polling. But they've been conveying to outside groups for weeks that they need help reinforcing vulnerable incumbents like Husted. On Monday, the pro-crypto super PAC Fairshake said it planned to unleash $30 million against Brown, who was the top Democrat on the Banking Committee before losing reelection in 2024 — fueled in part by more than $40 million against him from Fairshake that year.

"The stakes go far beyond one Senate seat," Amy Natoce, a Husted campaign spokesperson, said in a statement. "Control of the Senate will determine which agenda moves forward in Washington: Sherrod Brown's out-of-touch socialist agenda, or Jon Husted's agenda of lower taxes, a secure border, and an economy that rewards hard work."

One Michigan Republican acknowledged the immense weight of the tariffs in races across the battleground state — including in the marquee Senate contest between Rogers and progressive Abdul El-Sayed, as well as across competitive House races.

"Everywhere we go, we are getting hammered on it," the Michigan Republican said. "It's crushing us."

Even skeptical Republicans have been quietly checking in with their colleagues to see if the panic in redder territory is borne out in reality on the ground or just overblown polling. One GOP lawmaker who spoke to Hinson and her campaign team was somewhat surprised by their answers.

"It's real," that House Republican told POLITICO.

And POLITICO overheard a senior member of Kansas' Republican party leadership complaining about their state's tighter-than-expected race at the GOP's midterm convention in Dallas earlier this month. GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, the person said, was in some trouble even as Republicans tried to dismiss the seriousness of his Democratic challenger, Adam Hamilton.

Trump and Vance, meanwhile, continue to travel to states they won by double digits in 2024 to stump for Republican candidates, as Trump-aligned super PACs hammer the airwaves in far more red territory than blue.

Recently-formed super PACs aligned with MAGA Inc. — Trump's main spending vehicle that holds more than $400 million — have spent in 42 House districts so far, 30 defensive and 12 offensive. On average, they are spending in areas that voted for Trump by 7.9 points in 2024, according to a POLITICO analysis.

The PACs are even spending in some districts Trump carried by 15 points as a way to shore up Republicans and deter Democratic advances, according to Republicans involved in the conversations.

Major Republican super PACs, including the Trump aligned-super PACs and party-linked groups, have spent in more than two dozen GOP-held seats where Trump won by at least 5 points in 2024.

"Republicans aren't taking anything for granted this cycle and will deploy whatever resources necessary to protect our majorities and prevent Democrats from taking control," RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement.

The NRSC argued that "Democrats lack quality candidates and a clear path to victory," so the party is "feigning optimism" and looking to candidates who have lost before, including Brown, "to somehow deliver [a] majority." The NRCC said their opposition is "too broke to fight back."

The geography of the Senate map still favors the GOP this cycle: Democrats have to defend all of their seats, while flipping four Republican-held ones, to take control of the upper chamber.

Republicans believe they have a real shot at flipping New Hampshire , and public polling shows Minnesota's Senate race closer than expected, forcing Democrats to pay some minor attention to a state Kamala Harris won in 2024.

And Republicans are still hopeful that their mid-decade gerrymandering push could still give them a structural advantage as they fight to defend the House. Republicans won the redistricting war that erupted last summer and will likely net at least six seats from it.

But as economic concerns continue to dominate — with little relief in sight — Democrats are growing increasingly bullish.

"You know, I look at places like Kansas where I never thought we'd have a chance, or South Carolina or even Mississippi, these places are longshots, but they look like they're competitive," Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) said.

For their part, senior Republicans have been working the problem from two ends, trying to gently persuade Trump in private conversations to back off some of his recent policy moves and wind down the war in Iran — while also organizing a wave of cash reinforcements across the growing map to try to stem the bleeding.

GOP lawmakers pressed Trump officials at their Dallas convention and since then to take emergency actions around fuel prices and refinery capacity. A band of House Republicans led an unsuccessful attempt to vote on a federal gas tax suspension until after Election Day. And, over the weekend, Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) posted several direct appeals to Trump, asking why he hasn't put an embargo on diesel exports.

But many are convinced the bleeding won't stop until voters get some relief at the pump.

"The question is: How much longer can we go?" one senior House Republican said.

articles.title: Trump’s plan to militarize proposed arch raises new legal, safety concerns
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s push to convert his planned triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery into a military complex has complicated a required feder...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's push to convert his planned triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery into a military complex has complicated a required federal review process and raised new legal and safety concerns.

Trump unveiled his new national security rationale Sunday in a post on Truth Social, saying that the 250-foot-tall arch project - which he has framed for nearly a year as a tourist attraction - will now house drones, snipers and ammunition. The president said he was making the change at the request of the U.S. military.

Critics of the plan saw echoes of Trump's shifting security case for the White House ballroom, which the administration has used to defend that project in court. But while presidents have historically had some leeway to revamp the White House grounds, the arch would stand on federal parkland more than a mile away, where Congress has set stricter rules for construction.

"There is nothing that authorizes or justifies a massive arch, even if Trump tries to disguise it as a military facility," said Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the top Democrat on a House committee that oversees federal parkland. "This is cartoonishly illegal, but he's obviously trying to find a way to do it anyway."

Aviation experts warned Monday that using drones at the planned arch site - Memorial Circle, a roundabout near Reagan National Airport - could pose risks in the airport's crowded airspace.

"Anything you add to the airspace complicates the airspace and increases the operational risk," said Tom Lintner, a former safety official at the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

Other military and safety experts have questioned the implications of storing ammunition in the middle of a heavily used traffic circle and whether tourists could still enter the arch as previously planned.

Historic preservationists participating in a required federal review process said they could not move forward until the administration clarifies Trump's plans for the arch. Administration officials last week had asked Washington and Virginia's preservation offices to agree to a memorandum of agreement (MOA) by Monday as part of that process, and they invited other preservationists to participate.

"This MOA is DOA," Charles Birnbaum of the Cultural Landscape Foundation wrote in an email to the administration on Monday. An official for Washington's historic preservation office also wrote in an email that the office needed clarity on Trump's post. Both emails were shared with The Washington Post.

Administration officials have declined to offer further details about Trump's plans to convert the arch to a military complex. They have previously said that they will not begin construction on the arch until they have received "all necessary approvals."

But Trump has pushed his deputies to expedite the arch and other construction projects, particularly in the wake of a Supreme Court ruling on Aug. 31 that let him continue building his ballroom, according to two people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations. The ruling did not decide the merits of the case.

Spokespeople for the White House and Pentagon said on Monday that they had no additional information to provide beyond the president's social media post. A defense official, speaking on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue, said it was not clear if U.S. Northern Command, which oversees domestic military operations, has been asked to develop any related plans.

Military officials with Joint Task Force-National Capital Region, which oversees military operations to protect D.C., did not respond to requests for comment on Monday. Spokespeople for the Interior Department and the National Park Service also did not respond to questions about the project. The Federal Aviation Administration referred questions to the White House.

Until Sunday, the Trump administration had largely portrayed the arch as a prominent tourist attraction. Architectural plans posted by the National Park Service last month include a "ticket booth," a "family restroom" and other features atypical of any active military complex.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum mentioned that the arch would also offer a "military observation deck" in a social media post earlier this month.

The administration had already faced safety questions, in part because the 250-foot-tall structure would sit directly in National Airport flight paths. Aviation safety there has garnered significant attention since a 2025 collision between an Army helicopter and an American Airlines regional jet near the airport that killed 67 people.

On Friday, the FAA said it had determined that the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft, including at National Airport. That finding preceded Trump's announcement about drones, whose type and frequency of use remain unclear.

In its final study on the arch, the FAA said the proposed structure should feature "a nonstandard eternal flame" to make it noticeable to pilots. It also said the arch should be continuously floodlighted by searchlight projectors around its base.

Jeff Guzzetti, a former FAA and National Transportation Safety Board accident investigator, said having drones in the flight path of National would worsen the airport's congestion problem.

"Even not knowing how often these things are going to be used, it would certainly increase the risk of a collision with a commercial airliner," Guzzetti said.

Michael McCormick, coordinator of the Air Traffic Management program at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, said he expected the FAA would need to conduct another study.

"Whatever the drones are, no matter what, the FAA would have to approve their flight because it's civilian airspace," McCormick said. "It cannot be a unilateral decision by the Pentagon."

articles.title: Donald Trump's UNGA address sparks walkout by Iranian delegation
articles.summary: The president asked, “Do I drive [the Islamic Republic] into hell?”
articles.body:
President Donald Trump gave his highly anticipated U.N. General Assembly speech Tuesday morning in front of a standing-room-only crowd.

However, as Trump spoke about the last six months of Iran's military strikes , that country's U.N. delegates walked out of the assembly.

Trump told the gathering of world leaders in New York City that he had a "big decision" coming up on Iran.

"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" Trump asked.

"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" The president continued: "Do I drive them into hell?"

Trump said he believes Tehran will "make a deal right after the [midterm] election" in November.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi are in New York for the annual meeting but didn't attend Trump's speech. However, their staff and delegates watched the beginning of Trump's speech, then exited the General Assembly 10 minutes into his remarks. Only one Iranian delegate remained in the hall to listen to the U.S. president.

As Trump spoke about Iran, the camera panned to the lone remaining delegate from Iran, who glared stone-faced at the president.

Newsweek reached out to the Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs via email on Tuesday morning for comment.

Trump also said in his speech that he's not concerned about the war in Iran hurting Republicans in the midterm elections.

The election "doesn't even enter my mind" when it comes to Iran, he said.

A new NBC News poll found widespread skepticism toward the conflict, with 62 percent of voters saying the war has not been worth it and 57 percent saying they would be less likely to support candidates who back it. The findings arrive amid growing Republican unease over the war's political costs, particularly in competitive midterm races.

Diesel has risen to a record $6.50 amid ongoing supply constraints from the Iran war and other global pressures, exposing a significant political vulnerability for the GOP.

Still, Trump said he's not concerned with politics.

"They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election," Trump said of Iran. "What they don't realize is that I'm not running. I did that already, and won in a landslide … and I'll be here for two-and-a-half years."

The president also denied the U.S. military is running low on advanced weapons amid strikes on Iran.

"We have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using, and we're building them at levels that we have never done before," Trump said.

Some experts say stockpiles of Tomahawk cruise missiles, along with Patriot and THAAD missile interceptors, will take years to replenish.

"The United States has burned through Patriot, THAAD missile interceptors, and long-range strike missiles at an extraordinary rate," Kelly Grieco, senior fellow with the Stimson Center's Reimagining U.S. Grand Strategy Program, told Newsweek in July. "In the near term, this is a force-protection issue."

"Interceptors are what stand between Iranian missiles and American forces at bases across the Gulf," Grieco said. "This is the immediate risk, and it gets worse the longer this runs."

Trump Snaps at CNN's Kaitlan Collins Ahead of UNGA Speech Amid Media Ban

President Trump lashed out at CNN 's Kaitlan Collins before his address to the U.N. General Assembly in New York amid the White House ban to deny CNN, MS NOW and Politico access.

Those three news outlets are suing the president for violating the First Amendment .

Collins asked Trump as he entered the U.N. building, "Two-thirds of Americans don't think the U.S. is winning the war with Iran. When will it end?"

Arriving with First Lady Melania Trump, Trump brushed aside the question and told Collins: "You should not be here covering me. You said you weren't going to cover me. You shouldn't be covering me."

After Trump's comments, Collins said on CNN that the network "never said we were not going to cover the president" and vowed that CNN would continue reporting on him despite the White House's efforts to restrict its access. She noted that the network was covering the president from the United Nations under U.N. credentials while the legal fight over White House access continues.

The Associated Press contributed to this story.

Newsweek's reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here .

Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas

articles.title: Trump TV launches after White House bans CNN, MS NOW and Politico and major networks halt video coverage in protest
articles.summary: Major television networks suspended pool coverage of the president over the ban, which he defended as "an assault on the FAKE NEWS."
articles.body:
The fallout from President Trump's decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from the White House continued on Monday, with the news organizations filing a federal lawsuit, other outlets dropping their coverage in protest and the administration launching a live YouTube stream branded "TRUMP TV."

In response to the ban, four major TV networks — ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News — refused to participate in the White House pool, the rotating group of reporters, photographers and videographers that document the president's public events. CNN had been scheduled to serve as the television pool on Monday.

As a result, Trump was largely inaudible during a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the White House's new helipad on Monday, where he gave a brief speech without the microphone that the pool would typically provide.

On Monday night, the White House launched a Trump TV YouTube stream. Branded " TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station ," the White House said in its description that it would run videos and highlights of "the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place." The first video showed Trump's remarks on July 3 at Mount Rushmore.

The three banned news organizations filed a lawsuit against Trump and three of his top advisers in federal court earlier Monday, demanding that access for their reporters be immediately restored.

"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in a joint statement. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."

According to the complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., the news outlets allege that Trump and the White House are retaliating against them for coverage they dislike.

"President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration," the complaint states. "But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting."

The organizations argue that their reporters were not afforded due process and are asking a federal judge to quickly rule that Trump's ban is unconstitutional. The filing cites a 1977 ruling by the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, which found that the White House cannot arbitrarily deny a journalist a press pass without due process.

"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the filing states.

Trump appeared to respond to the lawsuit in a social media post early Monday.

"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America," the president wrote on Truth Social . "It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!"

A hearing was set for Wednesday. Trump indicated in a follow-up Truth Social post that he would appeal any ruling against him.

The White House released a statement on Monday afternoon, saying that access for journalists is "a privilege — not a right."

"The First Amendment protects their right to publish; it does not entitle them to a hard pass, briefing room seat, or place in the press pool," the statement read. "No President is required to host a hostile operation on the grounds. Access has always been a privilege — and President Trump is applying that rule."

On Friday afternoon, Trump announced the ban in a Truth Social post , saying it was not prompted by any particular stories but was "a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," Trump said at an Oval Office event an hour later while explaining his decision to enact "the ban on the free press."

"There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories," the president said. "If they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house."

According to CNN , Trump's close aide Natalie Harp showed him clips of media coverage shortly before he announced the ban.

On Saturday, reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were turned away from the White House by members of the Secret Service and had their credentials — so-called hard passes needed for access — confiscated.

The journalists — CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett — are listed as plaintiffs in the court filing.

The White House Correspondents' Association condemned the move, saying it violates the First Amendment.

"The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably," Jacqui Heinrich, Fox News senior White House correspondent and WHCA president, said in a statement . "That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."

On Sunday, Trump posted what appeared to be an AI-generated image of trash bags bearing the logos of CNN, MSNBC (MS NOW's former name) and Politico outside the White House.

The three news outlets are longstanding members of the White House press pool that provides rotating coverage of the administration and travels with the president.

The daily guidance issued by the White House for Monday listed no primary TV pool, identifying Hearst and Real America's Voice as the "secondary" TV crews for the president's events in Washington and his scheduled trip to New York City for the United Nations General Assembly.

The Washington Post , the New York Times and HuffPost each announced that they would not publish images of Trump's trip on Monday in solidarity with the banned journalists.

U.S. presidents throughout history have complained about negative coverage of their administrations. In 2009, the Obama administration sought to exclude Fox News from a series of interviews with a Treasury Department official in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, but backed down when the other major television networks objected.

Trump, however, has continued his adversarial relationship with the media, often referring to the press as the "enemy of the people."

In 2018, Trump administration officials revoked the press pass of then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta after they said that he had interrupted the president during a news conference. The network sued, and a federal judge ordered Acosta's credentials restored .

A similar situation played out the following year when the White House revoked Playboy correspondent Brian Karem's press pass over a verbal argument between Karem and Sebastian Gorka, a former White House aide, at a Rose Garden event. A federal judge ordered the White House to restore Karem's pass .

Last year, Trump barred Associated Press journalists from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some official events after the news service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Trump's preferred name, the Gulf of America. The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing.

In his first event without a network TV pool on Monday, Trump unveiled the White House's new helipad before departing for New York. His remarks were nearly inaudible on the White House video feed . Joe Reberkenny, a White House correspondent for the Washington Blade who was serving as the in-town pool reporter, said he couldn't hear Trump "over the sound of the helicopter."

articles.title: Leavitt pulls back the curtain on Trump's 'tense,' unfiltered private talks with Putin, Xi, Starmer
articles.summary: Karoline Leavitt revealed President Donald Trump's private talks with foreign leaders mirror his public stance, detailing tense calls with Putin, Xi and a blunt lunch with Starmer.
articles.body: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt described President Donald Trump’s approach to high-stakes diplomacy in a new interview Tuesday, recounting tense phone calls with foreign adversaries and a lunch with former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer. Speaking on the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast, Leavitt recalled how Trump spoke bluntly with foreign leaders during calls with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, as well as with allies like Starmer. "I sat in on a lunch with the president and Starmer. And we're sitting around the table, and we're all enjoying lunch. And we were in this beautiful place. And the president just starts ripping into him for his policies," Leavitt said. TRUMP SAYS UK'S STARMER WILL RESIGN, WISHES HIM WELL AMID REPORTS OF PM'S POLITICAL FUTURE "He's like, ‘Your policies here are so stupid. You need to close your borders,’" Leavitt added. "’You need to deport these people you have in your country. I know your country, I know your people, they hate what you're doing.’" Leavitt said Trump takes the same candid approach with allies and adversaries and argued that what he told the media about his conversations with foreign leaders mirrored what happened behind closed doors. TRUMP WAS A 'CAGED LION' ROARING TO RETURN TO WHCA DINNER BALLROOM AFTER SHOOTING, LEAVITT SAYS "What he says to the media publicly is exactly what he's saying behind the scenes privately, too. In fact, much of what he says privately at some point is going to become public when he speaks to the press, because he's just candid, and he's honest," Leavitt said. "What he says with these foreign leaders behind the scenes is exactly what he tells the media five minutes later when he does a press conference. There's no games," she added. BEHIND SUMMIT SMILES, XI GIVES BLUNT WARNING TO TRUMP OF 'CLASHES' AND 'CONFLICTS' In conversations with Putin and Xi, Leavitt described "tense" phone calls in which she witnessed the president being "very straightforward." When asked about Trump's language during these high-stakes moments, Leavitt said that while the president "curses a lot" in general, he keeps those specific translator-assisted calls direct and professional. "The president was very honest about the fentanyl coming into the country and the precursors to the fentanyl that were manufactured in China. And he brought that up as a sticking point and said, ‘You have to do something about that,’" Leavitt said of Trump's meeting with Xi in South Korea. TRUMP HEADS TO BEIJING FOR HIGH-STAKES XI TALKS AS TAIWAN TENSIONS, TRADE DISPUTES TEST US STRENGTH "And sure enough. You know, a couple weeks later, I think it was Kash Patel who announced that those precursors would no longer be sent here. So, you know, he demanded results on behalf of our country, and he made sure that they were delivered upon," she added. Leavitt said Trump also pressed China to buy more U.S. soybeans to support American farmers. TRUMP SAYS FIRST CALL WITH NEW UK PM BURNHAM WENT 'VERY WELL,' PLEDGES US SUPPORT "Sure enough after the meeting they did," she said. "So, he's always again advocating for what our country needs, what our people need, and he's unequivocal about that." In August, Leavitt announced her decision to leave her role at the White House to spend more time with her family. She gave birth to her second child in May. Leavitt wrote about the decision in a post on X: "Serving as the White House Press Secretary over the past year and a half has been the honor and adventure of a lifetime," Leavitt wrote. I have spoken with great pride about the many historic accomplishments of this Administration, and I have relished holding the liberal media accountable and ensuring the American people hear the truth about President Trump’s successes."

articles.title: GOP senator asks Senate committee to subpoena Donald Trump Jr., Hunter Biden
articles.summary: GOP Sen. John Curtis of Utah asked a Senate panel to subpoena Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden for testimony as part of a probe into the "use of presidential famil...
articles.body:
Washington — GOP Sen. John Curtis of Utah asked the Senate Judiciary Committee on Monday to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden for testimony regarding their business dealings, relationships with foreign individuals and entities and gifts they received, after recent revelations about a Russian oligarch's financial involvement in the wedding of President Trump's eldest son.

"A toaster is a wedding gift. A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else," Curtis said in a post on X. "Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden's foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now."

In a letter to Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley of Iowa and ranking member Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois, Curtis asked that the committee "launch an investigation into the use of presidential family relationships for private financial benefit, preferential treatment, or access by domestic and foreign interests." As part of that investigation, he urged the committee to subpoena the eldest son of President Trump and the son of former President Joe Biden.

Curtis pointed in the letter to Hunter Biden conducting "substantial business" with foreign entities, including in China and Ukraine, while his father was in office or seeking office. And he wrote that more recently, questions have surfaced about Donald Trump Jr.'s relationships with foreign business figures and "the acceptance of significant gifts."

"These include a lavish wedding afterparty, on a private island, provided by Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev, who reportedly traveled to China as part of a delegation accompanying Vladimir Putin shortly before giving the gift," Curtis wrote.

Last week, ProPublica published a story with the headline, "Donald Trump Jr.'s Bahamas wedding was secretly bankrolled by Russian oligarch close to Putin." In a post on Instagram, Bettina Anderson, the wife of Donald Trump Jr., confirmed that Kremlev had hosted some of their May post-wedding festivities on a private island in the Bahamas as "an extraordinarily generous wedding gift."

The Utah Republican has decried the gift from a Russian oligarch, saying on social media last week that "it just stinks — it's corruption." He called it a "big deal" and gave a video preview of his plan to call for congressional action.

Curtis wrote that, in addition to Trump Jr.'s promotion of the family's cryptocurrency ventures, pursuit of international real estate deals and ties to prediction-market platforms, among other things, the reports "raise legitimate questions about foreign access to members of a sitting president's family and whether such relationships can create actual or perceived expectations of favorable treatment."

"They also may create expectations of a returned favor that would not be in the best interests of the American people or our allies, and could even create national security vulnerabilities," he wrote.

Curtis said the purpose of the probe should be "straightforward: establish the facts, determine whether existing ethics, disclosure, or anti-corruption laws apply, and identify reforms necessary to prevent the presidency from becoming a vehicle for private enrichment by those closest to it."

"Americans deserve confidence that public institutions serve them — not presidents, political parties, wealthy interests, or members of powerful families," Curtis continued. "Congress has an obligation to pursue credible concerns wherever they lead and without regard to party."

Durbin, a Democrat, responded to the letter in a statement expressing his support, while saying corruption "at the highest levels of our government should never be tolerated."

"Senator Curtis has made a good faith request that the Senate Judiciary Committee investigate the lavish gift of a Russian oligarch to President Trump's son as well as any wrongdoing by the son of former President Biden," Durbin said. "In fairness, Hunter Biden has already given a sworn deposition to Congress on this issue of corrupt activity. Donald Trump Jr. has not. For the Committee to ignore this matter is to run the risk of being complicit in a coverup. I will join in supporting Senator Curtis' request of the Senate Judiciary Committee."

articles.title: In U.N. speech, Trump threatens to "annihilate" Iran and defends foreign policy
articles.summary: President Trump said he could "annihilate" Iran while predicting that Tehran would make a deal to end the war after the U.S. midterm elections.
articles.body:
Washington — President Trump defended his handling of conflicts around the world in a speech before the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, saying he could "annihilate" Iran while predicting that its leaders would make a deal to end the war after the U.S. midterm elections.

He framed his approach to foreign policy over his first two years back in office as deploying American power to solve "decades of intractable challenges" that previous U.S. leaders have failed to address.

"I do not believe in letting problems fester. They only become harder to solve. So while others have talked, I have acted," he said.

The roughly 35-minute speech came before Mr. Trump is set to meet with other world leaders on the sidelines of the annual U.N. gathering, including the prime minister of the U.K. and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He is navigating several ongoing international conflicts beyond the war with Iran, which will hit its seven-month mark next week. Mr. Trump is also seeking to close a peace plan for the Gaza Strip between Israel and Hamas , and has struggled to bring Russia's invasion of Ukraine to an end.

In his remarks, the president justified his decision to begin the war with Iran, framing it as an effort to prevent Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. After recounting the run-up to the war and the failed negotiations to end the fighting over the past several months, Mr. Trump said he has "a big decision to make."

"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world?" he said. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?"

"But I believe we'll make a deal, right after the election," he continued. "Because it doesn't make sense for them not to. They're waiting to see how I do on the midterm election. What they don't realize is that I'm not running."

The president said "the United States and Iran will definitely get it done — we will get it done, one way or the other." Mr. Trump also dismissed reports about diminished U.S. munition stockpiles, saying "we have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using." The Pentagon's own inspector general said last week that the war in Iran has led to "strategic inventory shortfalls" of munitions.

The president insisted in his speech that he has brought about peace in a way other world leaders could not, while settling years of "unfinished business."

"While others have talked, I have acted," he said. "While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them. While others have talked of courage, America has shown it. While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world."

The president also emphasized the United States' influence in the Western Hemisphere, particularly touting U.S. intervention in Venezuela and procurement of billions of barrels of Venezuelan oil.

"To the victor belong the spoils, you've all heard that," he said. "Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere, and if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States."

The president also touted the new security agreement he said the U.S. has reached with Greenland and Denmark, calling Greenland the "northern frontier of North America." The U.S., which already has a military presence in Greenland, will build two "major" military bases, he said. Mr. Trump said the agreement will be signed later Tuesday. Disputes over Greenland, trade, defense spending and Mr. Trump's push for NATO members to assist with the Iran war have frequently brought him into conflict with Canada and European states over the last year.

The president also continued his tirade against critics of the acceleration of artificial intelligence, while saying he's going to try to rebrand "AI" as "superintelligence" or "SI."

"Every major new technology brings challenges. And superintelligence is no exception," he said. "Yet, the very same people who said we'll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming … and nobody was dead. These are the same people that are now saying that AI is going to kill us all, that robots are going to attack us, and that everything is going to be a total disaster."

"I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," he added, insisting the U.S. will continue to lead the world "safely and responsibly."

Mr. Trump is scheduled to meet with a number of leaders on the sidelines of the General Assembly, including U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and various Gulf state leaders. He met with French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday. He's also expected to have a pull-aside conversation with acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez, about whom Mr. Trump has spoken positively since U.S. forces removed former leader Nicolás Maduro from power.

Mr. Trump is preparing to welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday for a high-stakes state visit. The tenuous U.S.-China relationship is lingering in the background of the General Assembly. American and Chinese negotiators have sought to mend their economic relationship after last year's tit-for-tat trade war, and have discussed opening up communications on the risks posed by artificial intelligence.

The U.S. president has praised Xi in spite of questions about Chinese entities assisting Iran and buying Russian oil. China is the world's largest buyer of Russian crude oil, potentially putting Beijing in the crosshairs of a law signed by Mr. Trump last week threatening heavy tariffs against Russia's largest energy customers.

Mr. Trump dismissed a report by the Wall Street Journal that Chinese entities provided Iran with satellite imagery of a base in Jordan used by U.S. troops before Iran killed three Americans there.

"I think he's behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well," Mr. Trump said last week of Xi's conduct during the war with Iran.

The president's movements and meetings at the U.N. won't be nearly as accessible for viewers as in past years.

After the White House banned Politico, CNN and MS NOW from the White House, the presidential network pool — consisting of ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC — suspended pool coverage of the president. That means there likely won't be television coverage of the president's meetings with foreign leaders. Politico, CNN and MS NOW announced they're suing the Trump administration, citing First Amendment concerns, in an effort to restore access.

Other cameras, however, are covering UNGA as a whole, and captured Mr. Trump on camera as he entered the building.

"You should not be here covering me," the president told a CNN reporter.

articles.title: Trump begs Ukraine and Russia to stop the war, save diesel
articles.summary: President Trump is to be commended for everything he has done to try and bring about peace. But the reality is that there’s only one person who can truly end this pointless, destructive war. That person is Vladimir Putin.
articles.body:
President Trump has a message regarding Russia’s war on Ukraine: He wants it to end! And he’s particularly irate about the price of diesel , now that Ukrainian long-range missile strikes are devastating Russia’s ability to produce it.

“Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine. A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission. This ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended. The whole World suffers as 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are being killed each month. What a shame! President DJT”

And he’s right, it’s a terrible shame. The war has been a disaster, and has resulted in the deaths of tens of thousands of people. It is also causing skyrocketing energy prices in Europe and for the U.S., and that’s bad.

But we know who to blame here: We must blame Russian President Vladimir Putin, who is at this point solely responsible for the fact that the war continues. We can’t really blame the Ukrainians for defending their country. They are being invaded, and they are trying to keep Russia at bay — rather successfully, I may add.

Ukraine is now effectively holding Russia’s forces back, and is using drone warfare and long-range missiles to punish the invaders. In response, Russia has launched devastating strikes on Kyiv aimed at trying to terrify the public into surrendering. But it isn’t working, as I learned firsthand during my trip to Ukraine: It is very apparent that the Ukrainians do not want to be part of Russia, and are willing to continue the fight for their independence.

So they are going to keep battling the Russians, until Russia decides to let Ukraine be. And for what it’s worth, Ukrainian President Volodmyr Zelensky is willing to agree to an immediate ceasefire along the current lines so that peace talks can take place. Ukraine wants to stop hitting Russian oil refineries, but they can’t stop unless Russia agrees to stop targeting Ukraine.

It’s simple: the defending party, Ukraine, can’t stand down unless the attacking party, Russia, agrees to stop attacking. Quite obviously.

In a response to Trump, Zelensky reiterated this stance, writing :

“Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part. Solutions are possible. We are ready to work on this, and we will discuss it with our partners on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.”

Indeed, Trump is to be commended for everything he has done to try and bring about peace. But the reality is that there’s only one person who can truly end this pointless, destructive war. That person is Putin.

He could end it tomorrow: Agree to a ceasefire, and have negotiations concerning the fate of the occupied territories. But he must agree not to try to conquer the rest of Ukraine, at the very least. And if he won’t do that, then the war is going to continue. And we will all suffer as a result.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Carville says Piker ‘not a Democrat’: ‘Don’t use our name’
articles.summary: Democratic strategist James Carville again went after left-wing streamer Hasan Piker on Monday, saying he is “not” a member of his party. “So, let me repeat: Hasan Piker is not a Democrat, OK?” Carville told Fox News’s Laura Ingraham on her show. “Hasan Piker is not a Democrat. I don’t really care what he says,”…
articles.body:
Democratic strategist James Carville again went after left-wing streamer Hasan Piker on Monday, saying he is “not” a member of his party.

“So, let me repeat: Hasan Piker is not a Democrat, OK? ” Carville told Fox News’s Laura Ingraham on her show.

“Hasan Piker is not a Democrat. I don’t really care what he says,” he added. “And, what my problem with the democratic socialists are, don’t use our name. If the Democratic name is held in such ill repute by the democratic socialists, Hasan Piker, call yourself something else. Call yourself the — I don’t care — call yourself the Communist Party, don’t matter to me.”

Piker has frequented national conversations in the last year as he has campaigned for insurgent progressive candidates who have defeated more establishment figures in their primaries.

He also has a history of controversial comments and has recently faced criticism from more moderate figures in the Democratic Party, like Rep. Jared Moskowitz (Fla.) and Sen. John Fetterman (Pa.).

Carville’s Monday swings at Piker are not his first.

“To talk about the larger Democratic Party, post the election in Michigan going forward, I am not going to be in the same party with Hasan Piker,” the Democratic strategist said last month while on Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing,” referencing the Michigan Senate race and Piker’s proximity to Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

“I have no intention of ever being in the same political party with that guy. Now, I think that a majority –– overwhelming majority of Democrats agree with me, but this idea that we’re going to seize the means of production and this –– just go look at the DSA platform,” he continued, referring to the Democratic Socialists of America.

Carville also took the time Monday to address a controversial figure across the aisle.

He commented on Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner Bo French, whose racist comments recently drew criticism from within the GOP.

“Bo French is a Republican, the person that said that only whites should go to the University of Texas,” Carville told Ingraham.

The Hill has reached out to Piker for comment.

articles.title: Collins opponent says ‘jig is up’ after ProPublica report; her aide calls it ‘categorically false’
articles.summary: Maine Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson criticized his opponent, Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), saying “the jig is up,” following a ProPublica corruption report into the senator which her aide calls “categorically false.” “This is corruption of the highest order. Susan Collins delivered millions in taxpayer dollars for a corrupt donor bankrolling her campaign, and then…
articles.body:
Maine Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson criticized his opponent, Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), saying “the jig is up,” following a ProPublica corruption report into the senator which her aide calls “categorically false.”

“This is corruption of the highest order. Susan Collins delivered millions in taxpayer dollars for a corrupt donor bankrolling her campaign, and then Donald Trump helped her cover it up,” Jackson wrote in a statement . “No wonder she voted with him 96% of the time and has rubberstamped his agenda to hurt Maine.”

“We deserve answers about every contract and every conversation that Collins and her team facilitated on the backs of taxpayers. The jig is up,” he added.

Collins’s Deputy Chief of Staff Annie Clark responded to the allegation on social platform X, calling the report, “categorically false.”

Clark said the Collins campaign had “cooperated fully with the FBI throughout the investigation” during the Biden administration and produced all documents and fact witnesses in official settings.

“There have never been any allegations of wrongdoing by the Collins for Senator campaign, and the campaign was never the target of the FBI investigation,” Clark wrote. “These issues were resolved in 2021, and the FBI has not contacted us about Martin Kao since then.”

The ProPublica report concerned a pay-to-play operation run by Hawaii-based defense firm Navatek’s executives and former CEO Martin Kao, who is currently in federal prison for COVID-relief wire fraud, money laundering and bank fraud.

The report alleged Collins, as chair of the Appropriations Committee, gave contracts worth millions of dollars to Navatek. It cited meetings between Collins super PAC head Scott Reed and Navatek executives at Corner Bakery where he solicited payments from the company.

In one instance, Kao reportedly sent $150,000 to Collins’s super PAC using a shell company — then two months later told Navatek executives that Collins would give the company $32 million in naval contracts.

When Kao was arrested, he told the FBI and Justice Department public corruption investigations team about the scheme, which they were prepared to investigate further until President Trump took office in 2025. ProPublica reported that the team responsible for handling Kao’s case left or were fired from the agencies for past investigations into Trump.

An FBI spokesperson told The Hill that “the allegations made in this article had already been investigated by the FBI years ago and ultimately found nothing implicating Senator Collins or Senator Collins’ campaign. Any suggestion otherwise is totally false.”

“Furthermore, as we have said repeatedly, personnel are only removed at this FBI if they have been found to have acted unethically, undermined the mission, or engaged in weaponization of law enforcement. Any suggestion otherwise is false,” the spokesperson continued.

articles.title: Paramount merger dangerous, Americans will be ultimate losers
articles.summary: Paramount just cleared one of the biggest hurdles standing between it and Warner Bros. Discovery.
articles.body:
Paramount just cleared one of the biggest hurdles standing between it and Warner Bros. Discovery.

The company has reached a settlement with California and 11 other states that sued to stop the roughly $110 billion merger, bringing these two Hollywood giants significantly closer to becoming one company.

Part of the agreement is reportedly that Paramount will create independent editorial boards for both CNN and CBS. It faces a $30 million penalty for every film it falls short on if it fails to meet its commitment to release 30 movies theatrically each year. Deadline reports that the agreement will also include investment in domestic film production, along with protections around California production and studio operations.

Paramount also settled with The Writers Guild of America, which sued to stop the deal, arguing it would decrease pay and worsen working conditions for film and television writers. But there are still plenty of underlying consequences of consolidation.

This deal would put an enormous collection of Hollywood’s most recognizable assets under one roof: Paramount Pictures, CBS, Paramount+, Warner Bros., HBO, HBO Max and CNN, BET and others.

Paramount has told investors it expects roughly $6 billion in cost savings from the combination. And in media, “efficiency” always translates into eliminating jobs immediately. That doesn’t just mean actors and writers. Think editors, camera operators, producers, production assistants, electricians, transportation workers and caterers.

And for people trying to break into this business, consolidation can mean fewer doors to knock on. As New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote earlier this year : “This is not a merger that serves the public. It would hand one company nearly a third of the movies and cable channels Americans watch, raise prices for streaming and cable, endanger the livelihoods of thousands of New York artists and entertainment workers, and threaten to shutter theaters across our city.”

Opponents of the merger have continued protesting and pushing state officials for stronger protections. There was a “Block the Merger” protest in New York just yesterday. But even if the job loss doesn’t bother you, the question about who owns the media Americans consume should.

The Federal Communications Commission just approved a structure allowing sovereign wealth funds from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates to collectively hold up to 49.5 percent of Paramount’s equity . Meaning foreign governments are becoming major financial stakeholders in a company that owns major American television and news properties.

Paramount is doing whatever it can to get this deal to the finish line, because the company has a financial clock ticking: Reuters reports the company faces a roughly $7 million-a-day fee to Warner Bros. shareholders after Sept. 30 if the transaction isn’t completed by then. But the real losers of rushing this thing will ultimately be the average American.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Trump failing to block China’s access to American AI technology, say senior Senate Democrats
articles.summary: A group of Senate Democrats on Tuesday said President Trump is failing to block China from accessing sensitive American technology to accelerate its development of artificial intelligence, ahead of the Chinese leader’s state visit to Washington this week. Trump must close loopholes that China has used to subvert U.S. export bans on sensitive American technology,…
articles.body:
A group of Senate Democrats on Tuesday said President Trump is failing to block China from accessing sensitive American technology to accelerate its development of artificial intelligence, ahead of the Chinese leader’s state visit to Washington this week.

Trump must close loopholes that China has used to subvert U.S. export bans on sensitive American technology, the lawmakers wrote in a joint statement obtained exclusively by The Hill.

It was signed by Democrats with senior positions on the Senate panels for the armed services, foreign affairs, intelligence and banking.

“China is accelerating its drive for AI dominance by exploiting weaknesses in the administration’s export controls to access advanced chips and manufacturing equipment,” they wrote.

“President Trump must reverse course. He must end China’s access to the advanced chips and manufacturing equipment it needs to build dangerous AI systems.”

The signatories included Senate Minority Leader Chuck Shumer (D-N.Y.), Sens. Chris Coons (D-Del.), ranking member for Senate Defense appropriations; Patty Murray (D-Wash.), vice chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee; Jack Reed (D-R.I.), ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee; and Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.), vice chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), ranking member of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and Andy Kim (D-N.J.), ranking member of the Subcommittee on National Security and International Trade and Finance, also signed the statement.

The lawmakers also pushed Trump to hold Xi to account for Chinese companies reportedly providing Iran with intelligence to target U.S. troops in the Middle East; confront Xi’s pressure campaign against Taiwan; and punish Beijing for its support to Russia in its war against Ukraine.

“We can’t let President Xi leave stronger than when he arrived. That is not diplomacy, it’s weakness,” the statement said.

The Democrats statement on AI echoes concerns also raised by Republican Rep. John Moolenaar (Mich.), who wrote to Trump last week urging greater U.S. scrutiny on export controls, and for him to block China the People’s Republic of China (PRC) from illegally accessing advanced AI products.

Moolenaar is the chairman of the House Select Committee on U.S. competition with China.

“The correct response is to slow down PRC AI development as much as possible by strengthening controls on advanced AI products, cutting off cloud services loopholes that allow PRC [People’s Republic of China] companies to easily dodge these restrictions, and most importantly, stopping exports of American and allied semiconductor manufacturing technology that the PRC needs for its plan to work,” Moolenaar wrote in the letter .

The chairman also issued a warning last month to the Trump administration to make sure chip manufacturers don’t send advanced logic chips to untrusted Chinese firms.

In November, Trump paused for one-year an expanded Commerce Department blacklist of companies prohibited from buying U.S. technology goods, including semiconductor manufacturing equipment, as part of a deal with China when he met Xi in South Korea.

The expanded blacklist included firms more than 50 percent owned by companies already sanctioned by the U.S., and largely targeting Chinese companies and subsidiary firms located in other countries.

Trump has also granted China permission to buy hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips, Nvidia’s H200, and small batches have reportedly started entering mainland China in August. Opponents of that deal say that the advantage it gives China in technology development is not worth the economic benefit to American companies.

articles.title: South Dakota GOP election official backs Democrat to succeed her
articles.summary: South Dakota Secretary of State Monae Johnson (R) said Saturday she supports Democratic candidate Terrence Davis in the race to succeed her, breaking with her party’s backing of Republican nominee Heather Baxter. Johnson lost the GOP nomination to Baxter at the state’s Republican convention in June “The secretary of state must consider the law, the…
articles.body:
South Dakota Secretary of State Monae Johnson (R) said Saturday she supports Democratic candidate Terrence Davis in the race to succeed her, breaking with her party’s backing of Republican nominee Heather Baxter.

Johnson lost the GOP nomination to Baxter at the state’s Republican convention in June

“The secretary of state must consider the law, the information available, the effect on county officials, the security of statewide systems, the rights of voters, the cost and workload created by a change, and whether the proposal can be implemented within the deadlines the law requires,” she wrote in a column published by the conservative blog South Dakota War College.

Johnson added that the job “also requires a willingness to review new information and change course when the evidence supports doing so.” She wrote that Davis’s background includes experience working in law enforcement, a criminal justice degree, a master’s degree in public policy and the pursuit of his doctoral work in law and policy.

“He has publicly identified transparency, voting rights and making government systems work for the people who use them as priorities of his candidacy,” she continued. “Those areas have a direct connection to the work of the secretary of state’s office.”

Johnson concluded by asking voters from both sides of the aisle to “look beyond the letter beside a candidate’s name,” and saying that Davis is best prepared for her job and serving with “seriousness, steadiness and integrity.”

Johnson previously refused to say whether former President Biden won the 2020 election when she ran for secretary of state in 2022, NBC News reported .

Candidates running for the role have emphasized election safety and security. Davis told The Washington Sun on Monday that trust in the state’s election system has been eroded by misinformation.

“I believe people want somebody they can trust. They want a government they can trust. That’s really what it boils down to,” Davis told the outlet “My concern is for the voters and the stakeholders here in the state of South Dakota. I trust our system, I trust our elections and I trust our people.”

Baxter slammed Johnson’s endorsement, stating on Monday that the secretary’s line about the “letter beside a candidate’s name” was “catchy,” but that party matters. She called for votes to be “verifiable by paper balloting,” for “state- and tribal-issued photo IDs and against same-day voter registration.

“A sitting secretary of state who asks Republicans to ignore their own nomination is also asking them to treat all of these standards as negotiable,” Baxter said in a statement . “This office is too important for a consolation prize. The next secretary of state will inherit statewide election systems, business services, statutory deadlines, county relationships, public records, notary commissions, and the public’s confidence, and stands third in line below the governor.”

Baxter vowed to work with state and federal election officials and use all other resources “to maximize efficiency and accuracy” with the outcome of South Dakota’s elections.

Democrats have not held statewide office in South Dakota since 2015. The state overwhelmingly voted for President Trump in the last three presidential elections .

articles.title: Trump officially makes Rubio national security adviser
articles.summary: President Trump has signed a commission permanently making Secretary of State Marco Rubio the national security adviser, according to a White House official. Rubio is the first person to hold both roles at the same time since Henry Kissinger. The development was first reported by MS NOW. Rubio had previously been serving in the role…
articles.body:
President Trump has signed a commission permanently making Secretary of State Marco Rubio the national security adviser, according to a White House official.

Rubio is the first person to hold both roles at the same time since Henry Kissinger.

The development was first reported by MS NOW .

Rubio had previously been serving in the role in an acting capacity following the departure of former national security adviser and current U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz.

Waltz left the position over a year ago in May 2025 after he became embroiled in the scandal known as “ Signalgate ,” where he created a private group chat on the encrypted messaging app Signal in which high-ranking officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Vice President Vance, discussed military plans against the Houthis in Yemen.

Rubio has been praised by many in the administration, including Trump, as someone who is able to juggle multiple responsibilities.

“When I have a problem, I call up Marco. He gets it solved,” Trump said last year after he tapped Rubio to replace Waltz in an acting capacity.

Rubio has also been floated as a potential 2028 Republican presidential contender , along with Vance.

Rubio said earlier this month that he currently has no plans to launch a White House bid.

“I don’t know what the future holds, but I have no plans at this time,” Rubio said in an interview with Colombian news station RCN, translated by NBC News. “I’m not a candidate for anything right now. And I’m 100 percent focused on my job, and I have to be because I have two jobs.”

articles.title: Rubio’s meme-worthy job collection takes new turn with permanent Trump upgrade
articles.summary: Trump signed a commission making Secretary of State Marco Rubio his permanent national security adviser, a dual role unseen since the 1970s.
articles.body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio has collected an unusually broad portfolio in President Donald Trump’s second administration — and one of his most powerful roles is now permanent. Trump recently signed a commission formally making Rubio his national security adviser, a senior State Department official, White House official and senior administration official confirmed to Fox News Digital on Tuesday. The move makes permanent a role Rubio has held since May 2025, when Trump tapped him to replace Michael Waltz on an interim basis. I SERVED AS TRUMP’S NSA. SCOTUS NEED TO STOP COURTS PUTTING THE PRESIDENT'S SECURITY AT RISK Rubio will continue to manage the National Security Council process and serve as a direct line to the president on national security matters. The former Florida senator has been a prominent figure in the Trump administration, holding multiple official posts while becoming the subject of online jokes about just how many jobs he could take on. The move puts Rubio in rare company, being only the second person in U.S. history to simultaneously serve as secretary of state and national security adviser, after Henry Kissinger held both posts under President Richard Nixon in the 1970s. WHAT RUBIO’S RISE AS THE INTERNET’S 'FIXER' TELLS US ABOUT TODAY’S POLITICS Kissinger became Nixon’s national security adviser in 1969, later being sworn in as the secretary of state in 1973. The roles gave him extraordinary influence during the conflict with the Soviet Union, the opening to China and diplomacy surrounding the 1973 Arab-Israeli War. Trump has previously tapped Rubio to serve as U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) acting administrator shortly after being sworn in at the State Department. He was also tapped to serve as acting archivist of the United States, a post he held from February to December 2025. MARCO RUBIO GETS 68 NEW JOBS IN EPIC WHITE HOUSE BIRTHDAY GIFT INSPIRED BY VIRAL MEME Rubio has taken social media by storm, as critics and allies of the administration share viral memes showing doctored photos of Rubio sitting in the Oval Office wearing various outfits to fit a new job role he could pick up. articles.title: Christie mulls 2028 White House run amid bleak midterm outlook
articles.summary: Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie (R) on Tuesday said he’s considering a third presidential run in 2028 as the Republican Party faces a bleak midterm outlook. Christie, a onetime Trump ally who ran against him for the GOP nomination in 2024, questioned whether the party will decide it needs to change its approach or…
articles.body:
Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie (R) on Tuesday said he’s considering a third presidential run in 2028 as the Republican Party faces a bleak midterm outlook .

Christie, a onetime Trump ally who ran against him for the GOP nomination in 2024, questioned whether the party will decide it needs to change its approach or “the dominant wing” of the party, “if we do a lot of losing six weeks from today.”

“So, am I looking at it? Look, anybody who comes up here, anybody who comes up here and has ever run for president and not one and told you they’re not looking at it again is lying. …,” he said at the Granite State Summit on Responsible Gaming , per footage shared by WMUR 9’s Adam Sexton.

He added, “Once you go through the thought process of convincing yourself that you can be president, and then the next step that you should be president, that doesn’t leave your brain.”

“So, the way I look at this is, if I’m going to go back home to my wife and say, ‘I know you may not believe this, but third time is the charm,’ like, I better have a real theory,” the former governor continued. “And what she has said to me is, ‘Chris, I want to see the path.'”

Democrats are now favored to win the House and, more narrowly, the Senate this fall, according to the latest forecasts from Decision Desk HQ — amid problematic approval numbers for the president and growing voter anger over the economy under a Republican-led Washington.

As Trump serves out his second term, attention has already turned to 2028 as both major parties search for their next standard-bearer.

Vice President Vance has long been seen as the GOP heir apparent , and generated buzz when he gave a closing-night address to the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention earlier this month. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also seen his stock rise, and Trump has appeared to float both men for the post in the past.

Christie, who ran in 2016 and 2024, has long declined to rule out another bid, saying that he’ll wait to see the 2026 results before deciding whether to enter the ring.

articles.title: Vance, Oz chuckle about CNN, Politico ban during fraud event
articles.summary: Vice President JD Vance took a jab at two of the networks that President Trump banned from the White House during a Tuesday event for his fraud task force with Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS). “I have my notes here that I’m supposed to take questions…
articles.body:
Vice President JD Vance took a jab at two of the networks that President Trump banned from the White House during a Tuesday event for his fraud task force with Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS).

“I have my notes here that I’m supposed to take questions from CNN and Politico. Anybody from CNN and Politico here? No? OK,” Vance said with a smile.

The comment elicited a laugh from Oz, who stood behind him. The vice president turned to give the CMS administrator a thumbs up.

Trump announced in a Friday Truth Social post that he was barring CNN, POLITICO and MS NOW from the White House, “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”

The president did not provide a reason for the timing of this ban, telling reporters in the Oval Office Friday afternoon the decision was based on “cumulative stories” over the course of his second term.

During his arrival at the UN General Assembly in New York City on Tuesday morning, the president remarked that he was “ surprised ” to see CNN’s chief White House correspondent, Kaitlan Collins, in the crowd of reporters.

“You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to be covering me,” he told the reporter.

Collins later clarified on air that she was credentialed for the event under the UN and emphasized the network “never said we were not going to cover the president.”

MS NOW, Politico and CNN filed a joint lawsuit against the administration on Monday, in which attorneys for the outlets claimed the president’s action amounted to a “direct assault on the First Amendment” and a “blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles.”

Trump defended his media ban in a Monday evening Truth Social post .

“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” the president wrote. “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio echoed the president’s defense during a Tuesday morning appearance on NBC News’s “TODAY” show.

“I don’t think the White House is saying they’re not able to cover the President,” Rubio told host Craig Melvin.

“What he is arguing is, why should I have these people? What right do they have to be embedded in this building?” the secretary added. “They can cover the White House; they just can’t have a desk there.”

On Monday evening, the White House also announced its own 24/7 streaming service on YouTube, called Trump TV.

The White House’s official social media account advertised the page as a place to find “top past moments, announcements and the latest and greatest from the administration all in one place.”

“Not every big moment has made it on your tv, now it can,” the post added.

Additionally, the administration will be employing additional verification for another 419,000 people.
