"To put into context the amount of money that we're stopping from going to fraudsters today, $2.2 billion, the average American child receives about $4,000 in health care benefits every single year. That means that we are saving 550,000 American children's worth of healthcare that was going to fraudsters and now will go to the essential services for which it was meant to go." VANCE TO HOST CONGRESS AT WHITE HOUSE TO DISCUSS LEGISLATIVE ACTION ON FRAUD Vance criticized the administration of former President Joe Biden for incentivizing Obamacare fraud, arguing that the administration's incentives for brokers to enroll people in the program, combined with relaxed eligibility for the program, became the perfect recipe for rampant fraud. WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE "In one case we found a fraud ring that had 40 agents, 40 brokerage agents who had funneled 50,000 people into the Obamacare system fraudulently. Now, some of those people were probably legitimate. Most of those people were not eligible (because) either they didn't meet the citizenship or the income requirements. Many of those people quite literally didn't even exist." Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and a member of Vance's Fraud Task Force, further expanded on the non-existent individuals fraudulently entered into Obamacare. DR. OZ NAMES 5 STATES IN FRAUD CRACKDOWN AS TRUMP ADMIN TARGETS MEDICAID ABUSE "Normally 1%, a single digit, 1% of people who get Obamacare exchange plans do not have a Social Security number," Oz said. "We're supposed to check their tax returns to make sure they're making between one and four times the poverty level, so they're eligible for all of our taxpayers to pay their insurance so they get the discount. Now, if 100% of people coming on the program don't have Social Security numbers, I think we'd all agree there's a problem," he continued. TRUMP ADMIN UNCOVERS 7,100% SURGE IN MEDICARE SKIN SUBSTITUTE CLAIMS, SAYS FRAUD CRACKDOWN BLOCKED MILLIONS Oz then revealed that over 1.1 million people who enrolled in Obamacare this year had no Social Security numbers. He also revealed that 35% of enrollees have never used the program. "They haven't bought a prescription medication. They haven't seen a doctor. That's just not possible. That's at least twice as much as your normal incidence of people having insurance and not using it. So, we know there is fraud," he added. He then detailed the case of convicted fraudster Cory Lloyd, who he said has "a very punchable face." Lloyd and his partner, Stephen Strong, preyed on vulnerable consumers to enroll them in Obamacare in a scheme to collect commission payments from insurance companies, according a February announcement from the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ). "These crooks bribed homeless and jobless people into enrolling in the ACA plans. They had no idea what they were doing," Oz said. Oz read text messages between Lloyd and Strong in which the pair schemed to enroll people who had lost their homes from hurricanes in Florida. "This is the text message. This is ... I can't even say these words on television. But Lloyd said 'it's a killer idea to sign up these poor individuals, make them victims. If it could pull it off. I want to rape the shelters.' And then Strong said, 'ha ha, not kidding. And then Lloyd said 'me either. Let's ef 'em up,'" Oz relayed. The pair were both convicted of one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States, according to the DOJ. Strong was also convicted of two counts of money laundering. Both were sentenced to a total of 20 years in prison and ordered to pay $180.6 million in restitution, according to the DOJ announcement. articles.title: San Francisco sues over delayed Trump social media posts
articles.summary: The city of San Francisco sued Truth Social’s parent company Monday over delayed Truth Social posts made by President Trump that users can receive early access to if they pay $100,000. The city’s attorney, David Chiu, argued that Trump Media & Technology Group (TMTG) violated California’s Unfair Competition Law, a state law against insider trading.…
articles.body:
The city of San Francisco sued Truth Social’s parent company Monday over delayed Truth Social posts made by President Trump that users can receive early access to if they pay $100,000.

The city’s attorney, David Chiu, argued that Trump Media & Technology Group (TMTG) violated California’s Unfair Competition Law, a state law against insider trading.

The lawsuit alleges that the company set the price for early access to make financial gains for itself while wealthy traders view government information before the public does.

“These everyday investors are placed at a substantial disadvantage to sophisticated firms willing and able to pay extraordinary sums for advanced access to market-moving information,” Chiu wrote in the lawsuit. “Trump Media’s scheme is unprecedented in its monetization of nonpublic information obtained through government service and sold on the private market.”

TMTG announced in July that it would launch “Truth API” as a direct data feed to give investment firms “real-time access to posts from the highest-ranking Truth Social accounts.” The company also pitched a discounted $60,000 plan if client firms agree to a three-year contract.

The lawsuit points to one Truth Social post as an example of Trump’s social media posting moving the stock market. The post, which went up on April 9, 2025, reads: “THIS IS A GREAT TIME TO BUY!!!” The post went live before Trump placed a 90-day pause on tariffs, and the stock market increased in value later that day.

“In fact, there are numerous examples where Trump’s announcement of a policy decision or official government information on Truth Social –– information that, until the post, was nonpublic, influenced financial, securities and other trading markets,” the lawsuit reads.

Trump is the largest shareholder in the company and Truth Social’s co-founder after other tech giants banned him from their social media platforms directly after the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. The platforms have since allowed him back.

The Hill has reached out to TMTG for comment.

“The people of California should outsource their future lawsuits to AI chatbots who, unlike the left-wing activists masquerading as attorneys who filed this lawsuit, will grasp the basic distinction between public and nonpublic information,” a TMTG spokesperson told The New York Times.

Chiu’s lawsuit included criticism from bipartisan lawmakers against the “Truth API” plan. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) told The Hill in July, after losing his primary to a Trump-backed candidate earlier this year, that he thought the plan was “wrong” and “a form of buying access.”

“Think it through,” Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) previously said. “You are talking about the ability to move markets when you’re advancing information. This is where we’re getting $100,000 for you to buy your visa to be a teacher in a place like Alaska. We don’t really want to be that place where everything comes down to pay for play.”

articles.title: US, Iranian officials hold three-hour meeting at UN: Trump
articles.summary: President Trump said Tuesday that U.S. officials had a three-hour long meeting with Iranian officials on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Trump described it as a “very good meeting, very productive meeting” when asked about it during his bilateral meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the Ukrainian delegation.…
articles.body:
President Trump said Tuesday that U.S. officials had a three-hour long meeting with Iranian officials on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

Trump described it as a “very good meeting, very productive meeting” when asked about it during his bilateral meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the Ukrainian delegation.

The president said another meeting is scheduled in the “very near future,” but didn’t give any further details.

“I can’t imagine why they wouldn’t want to do it,” he said of a potential deal between the U.S. and Iran that would the the fighting, which began at the end of February. “It’s greatness, potential greatness, or obliteration.”

He offered Kushner and Witkoff to comment on the meeting but didn’t confirm who exactly attended.

“I feel very good right now,” Witkoff told reporters.

Trump added: “They had a very good meeting, and we’ll see how it turns out. But certainly, it’s to their advantage to make a deal.”

Earlier during his General Assembly speech, the president said he has a “big decision to make.”

“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world,” he said. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again.”

He also predicted that a deal could be reached between the two countries after November’s midterm elections.

“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realize is that I’m not running. I did that already, and won in a landslide,” he said, noting that he still has two and half years more in his term.

He said the midterms do not “even enter my mind.”

“The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon,” the president said.

His comments come as the peace negotiations with the U.S. and Iran remain at a complete standstill and energy prices continue to rise as a result of the war. The high oil and gas prices, in addition to high fertilizer prices, have created headwinds for GOP congressional candidates.

articles.title: Trump deflects on whether White House will follow court decision on banned media
articles.summary: President Trump declined to say whether the White House will follow a court decision if a district court judge rules against his ban on three media outlets. During a bilateral meeting at the United Nations General Assembly with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Trump was asked, “If the district court decides against you, will you…
articles.body:
President Trump declined to say whether the White House will follow a court decision if a district court judge rules against his ban on three media outlets.

During a bilateral meeting at the United Nations General Assembly with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Trump was asked, “If the district court decides against you, will you let the three media outlets back in?”

“It probably will, because this is a judge who is not a particularly fair judge,” Trump responded to the question from Reuters.

“I think we have a right to clean out fake news,” he continued. “And by the way, they said they weren’t going to be here, but they came. I knew that would happen.”

The three major broadcast networks and Fox News announced they would not participate in the White House TV pool in solidarity with CNN, which is among the three banned outlets. None of the outlets said they would not cover Trump’s address and meetings at the UN.

Trump went on to say that when news is fake, “it’s actually dangerous,” and said he has “a right to clear it out.”

He did not say whether the administration would abide by the ruling from U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, whom Trump nominated to the federal bench in the nation’s capital during his first term. A tele-hearing in the case has been scheduled for Wednesday afternoon.

Kelly decided in CNN’s favor during a similar fight during Trump’s first term, when the White House revoked the access of correspondent Jim Acosta.

The president announced last week that CNN, MSNOW, and Politico were banned from covering the White House. The three outlets, in turn, sued the administration.

When asked to clarify why their reporting was dangerous, Trump accused outlets of making “false statements about the war” and of not having sources.

“It’s very dangerous for our country, and I won’t stand for it,” he said.

In a joint statement announcing their lawsuit on Monday, the three outlets said, “the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.”

“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting,” the statement continued. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”

articles.title: Sabato’s Crystal Ball moves 3 Senate, 4 gubernatorial races in Democrats’ favor
articles.summary: Larry Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved three Senate and four gubernatorial races to the left on Tuesday, citing the “persistently poor national environment” for the GOP ahead of the midterms. The Center for Politics at the University of Virginia’s election handicapper moved the Iowa Senate race from “Leans Republican” to “Toss-up,” the Kansas Senate race from…
articles.body:
Larry Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved three Senate and four gubernatorial races to the left on Tuesday, citing the “persistently poor national environment” for the GOP ahead of the midterms .

The Center for Politics at the University of Virginia’s election handicapper moved the Iowa Senate race from “Leans Republican” to “Toss-up,” the Kansas Senate race from “Likely Republican” to “Leans Republican” and the Michigan Senate race from “Toss-up” to “Leans Democratic.”

The crystal ball also shifted two gubernatorial races from “Leans Republican” to “Toss-up”: in Nevada, where Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) is seeking reelection, and Ohio, where Vivek Ramaswamy (R) and Amy Acton (D) are battling to succeed Gov. Mike DeWine (R).

The election handicapper also moved the Texas and Florida gubernatorial races from “Likely Republican” to “Leans Republican,” as Republicans attempt to hold on to those governor’s mansions.

Adding to the concerns for the GOP is that the crystal ball shifted three House races toward Democrats — the reelection bids for Reps. María Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) and Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa), as well as the matchup between Alex Mealer (R) and Leticia Gutierrez (D) in Texas’s redrawn 9th Congressional District.

The election handicapper still favors Salazar and Mealer, but now favors Democrat Christina Bohannan in her bid to unseat Miller-Meeks.

Salazar made waves last week when she released a campaign ad criticizing the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement policies but has since said the president has been “very receptive” to her warnings about Hispanic voters. Trump has also said Salazar still has his endorsement.

“A persistently poor national environment for Republicans informs several rating changes this week toward Democrats,” the crystal ball’s Kyle Kondik wrote.

Democrats need to flip a net of four Senate seats and three House seats to retake majorities in each chamber. Decision Desk HQ favors them to do so, giving Democrats 53 percent and 71 percent chances to wrestle back control of the upper and lower chambers, respectively.

The only Senate race Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted that Democrats are trying to hold serve in is in Michigan, where progressive Abdul El-Sayed (D) is taking on former Rep. Mike Rogers (R).

While Kondik noted he believes El-Sayed “will underperform what a Democratic Senate candidate could or should get in Michigan” this year, the former Wayne County health official remains a “soft favorite” to beat Rogers.

articles.title: Melania Trump says country entering ‘technological revolution,’ announces new Fostering the Future Together push
articles.summary: Melania Trump says the country is experiencing “an extraordinary moment in human history” at the “threshold of a technological revolution,” as she touted new events and partnerships as part of her Fostering the Future Together initiative. “Fostering the Future Together is a global coalition with a unified mission: to empower children through technology and education,”…
articles.body:
Melania Trump says the country is experiencing “an extraordinary moment in human history” at the “threshold of a technological revolution,” as she touted new events and partnerships as part of her Fostering the Future Together initiative.

“Fostering the Future Together is a global coalition with a unified mission: to empower children through technology and education,” the first lady said Tuesday in remarks in New York during the United Nations General Assembly. Representatives from countries including the U.K., Korea, the Philippines, Canada, Panama and Ukraine, and others were among those attending the event, according to the White House.

“Ideas once confined to science-fiction novels and films have become part of our everyday reality. What once seemed impossible is becoming ordinary,” Trump said.

“Artificial intelligence is transforming entire business sectors and it’s expanding how humanity accesses the largest corpus of information ever available to humanity,” she said.

“But access alone is not empowerment. We must give our children the tools — and teach them how to use those tools wisely,” she said.

Trump announced that she would host a Fostering the Future Together event at this December’s Group of 20 summit, scheduled to take place at President Trump’s golf resort near Miami.

The first lady also unveiled other gatherings tied to her education and technology-focused initiative, which she launched last year, including at the upcoming ASEAN conference in Manila hosted by Phillipines’ first lady Liza Araneta Marcos, as well as European and Caribbean regional conferences in the coming months hosted by Polish first lady Marta Nawrocka and Saint Kitts and Nevis first lady Diani Prince-Drew.

“To the leaders of these great nations: thank you for stepping forward to activate your regions. You will have my full support,” Trump said.

Trump also thanked several tech companies — including Amazon, Google, Adobe, Starlink, Intel and Zoom — who she said “have also stepped up to empower our children” through partnerships with Fostering the Future Together. Some of the support from the tech companies includes offering free AI-generated education tools for students and educators and expanding internet access, according to the State Department.

“Years from now, our children may not remember the meetings we held or the speeches we gave. But they will live with the consequences of what we do here,” Trump said, after noting 57 countries are now participating in her initiative.

“Let history say that at a moment of extraordinary possibility, leaders from around the world came together through Fostering the Future Together and chose to put children first,” she said.

articles.title: Mark Kelly: US military ‘doesn’t need more testosterone’
articles.summary: Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) bluntly criticized Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth Tuesday, denouncing the changes he has made to department leadership during his tenure. The retired Navy captain rebuked the secretary as “a guy who runs around on the stage, yelling about killing people and maximum lethality and testosterone” during an appearance on MS NOW’s “Morning…
articles.body:
Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) bluntly criticized Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth Tuesday, denouncing the changes he has made to department leadership during his tenure.

The retired Navy captain rebuked the secretary as “a guy who runs around on the stage, yelling about killing people and maximum lethality and testosterone” during an appearance on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” show.

“U.S. military doesn’t need more testosterone; it needs better leadership at this point,” the Democratic senator said. “The consequences of firing all of these admirals and generals is we’re losing a portion, a good portion, of a generation of great leadership.”

The testosterone comment follows new guidance released by the Pentagon last week to require mandatory screenings for testosterone deficiencies in male active-duty and reserve service members over the age of 30.

This is the latest in Hegseth’s efforts to ensure soldiers are on the “leading edge of lethality.”

Kelly pointed to the ousters of Gen. Chris Donahue , Gen. CQ Brown , Adm. Lisa Franchetti and Gen. Randy George , saying they were “fired for not being sufficiently loyal.”

“These are people that have decades — 30, 35 years — of experience,” Kelly said. “People we need to ensure our national security, and now my sense is he’s looking for people who are loyal to him, a secretary of defense, and the president.”

Kelly said it will take “a lot of time and effort to recover” from the loss of these military leaders.

“This has been an incredibly challenging time for the department, and the first step here is get rid of the secretary of Defense, who clearly has no idea what he is doing,” Kelly said.

Earlier this month, retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis (N.C.) called on President Trump to fire Hegseth after Army Secretary Dan Driscoll announced his resignation following reported clashes with the defense secretary over these leadership changes.

“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis posted on social platform X . “He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force.”

Additionally, GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.) introduced a resolution in the U.S. House last week to impeach Hegseth and claimed Republican leaders cut the legislative calendar short to avoid a vote on this measure.

The Kentucky Republican, who lost his reelection bid to a Trump-endorsed GOP challenger earlier this year, accused the defense secretary of violating “his oath to support and defend the Constitution of the United States.”

Andy Beshear (D), one of the many Democratic names floated as a possible 2028 White House contender, said Monday that his new book is not an indication of a presidential run. “A lot of politicians who write books seem to be potentially considering a presidential run,” CNN’s Kaitlan Collins said in an interview…
articles.body:
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D), one of the many Democratic names floated as a possible 2028 White House contender , said Monday that his new book is not an indication of a presidential run.

“A lot of politicians who write books seem to be potentially considering a presidential run,” CNN’s Kaitlan Collins said in an interview with Beshear on “The Source.” She added that fellow Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said he would not run in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris chooses to and asked if there were any names Beshear would not run against if they announced a campaign.

“Well, I haven’t made any decision on that, but I will say, I didn’t write this book for anything in the future. I wrote this book because I was tired of people hijacking faith to hurt people instead of to help people,” Beshear responded.

The Kentucky governor’s book, “Go and Do Likewise,” came out Tuesday. The governor said in a post on the social platform X that it is “about reclaiming faith as a force for good and providing hope in these chaotic times.”

Beshear was seen as a possible running mate for Harris back in 2024 before the role ultimately went to Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D). The Kenucky governor is notable in his role as a Democrat in a deep-red state, and his political profile has risen in the last couple of years.

In May, Beshear said that he was “comfortable” being referenced as a potential Democratic contender in the next presidential race. He told MS NOW’s Ali Vitali that he would not come to a final choice on whether to get into the race until he finishes his term as chair of the Democratic Governors Association.

“But I certainly at least want that conversation that’s out there to be one that’s focused, to where whoever is the nominee can win,” Beshear said at the time. “This election for Democrats isn’t a need to win; it’s an absolute have to win.”

articles.title: ICE tried to stop man before fatal Michigan car crash, police say
articles.summary: A fatal car crash in Michigan over the weekend happened after Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents tried to stop the driver, Grand Rapids police said Tuesday.
articles.body:
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. ( WOOD ) – A fatal car crash in Michigan over the weekend happened after Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents tried to stop the driver, Grand Rapids police said Tuesday.

ICE agents were the first to respond to the scene of the crash Sunday, neighbors told Nexstar’s WOOD .

Relatives confirmed that the man who died was Mario David Coronado Juarez, an undocumented immigrant from Guatemala who had lived and worked in Grand Rapids for about seven years.

In a release Tuesday, the Grand Rapids Police Department (GRPD) said ICE agents “attempted to stop the involved vehicle and the driver fled” at some point before the 7 a.m. crash.

A separate release issued by the GRPD about two hours after the crash reported that “officers responded to the area of Century Avenue SW and McKendrick Street SW for a car that had crashed into a tree and then caught fire.” GRPD said that the man, the only person in the car at the time, died on the scene.

“About seven o’clock, we hear a ‘boom,'” a neighbor told WOOD. “It was like a sonic boom. So then I got up [and] looked outside; it was the car smoking, and all the cars parked in both different ways. coming this way and the other way. So at first we thought it was … an undercover chase, but it was not. It was immigration.”

The neighbor, who recorded video of the scene on Century SW near McKendrick, pointed out what appeared to be unmarked law enforcement vehicles. Multiple individuals wearing what looked like bulletproof vests stood near the scene.

“Right here, see? That’s not a police car,” he said, pointing to an unmarked tan sedan in a video taken on his cellphone. “That’s immigration right there, too. … There were about seven to nine vehicles unmarked.”

The witness said that police and fire officials arrived after the unmarked vehicles, at which time a fire truck parked in front of the scene on the east side of Century SW at McKendrick, effectively blocking the neighbors’ views.

“We know immigration [is] trying to get everybody out of here and that’s not right,” the neighbor continued. “Because … [Coronado Juarez] was a construction guy, finishing houses and stuff like that … [ICE] try to treat them like criminals, when they’re not.”

Relatives of the deceased man said Coronado Juarez left family behind in Guatemala, including his children, so he could work in the U.S. and send money back home.

A family friend who did not want to be identified by name remembered him as a “good person,” adding, “He doesn’t bother people. He just works, goes home. He sends money to his family in Guatemala. His kids.”

In the Tuesday release, a GRPD spokesperson said it had requested the Michigan State Police’s assistance with the investigation.

“GRPD’s traffic unit investigators are limited in their ability to gather information from federal agents about events preceding the crash,” the spokesperson said. “Due to the complexity of the investigation, Chief Trigg has requested that the Michigan State Police take part in the investigation. MSP, under the direction of the governor and attorney general, may be in a better position to determine the timeframe and any other potentially relevant circumstances, and any next steps that may be appropriate.”

Grand Rapids police said they had no previous knowledge or involvement in the situation before being called to the crash site.

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to WOOD’s request for comment.

articles.summary: Rep. articles.body:
Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fl.), the GOP’s gubernatorial nominee in Florida and a close ally of President Trump, has removed certain mentions of the president’s name on his website’s new layout.

In the old layout , a banner at the top of Donalds web page said: “Chip in to Support Trump Endorsed Byron Donalds” with text below it saying, “TRUMP-ENDORSED.”

If users scrolled down, another bar highlighted the endorsement, alongside a photo of the president.

The new layout only shows Trump’s endorsement in a box next to other endorsements Donalds has received from SpaceX Founder Elon Musk, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), among others.

A source from the campaign told The Hill that the president is still “all over the website” and that Trump’s endorsement “is worth its weight in gold, and we are grateful to have it.”

The policy agenda on the website also shifted, with affordability listed as the first issue on the page instead of “Enact the Trump Agenda.”

When asked about the changes, a spokesperson from the Donalds campaign told The Hill, “Our campaign website reflects Byron’s focus on the issues that matter most to Floridians — affordability, insurance costs, and government transparency.”

“He’s running to be the next Governor of Florida, is proud to have President Trump’s endorsement, and has real policy proposals to tackle those issues,” the spokesperson continued.

Donalds’s website change comes as Republicans inch closer to what looks like it could be a difficult election day for the party. Trump’s approval ratings have fallen in a number of polls, hitting a low of 35 percent in the Economist and YouGov poll released Tuesday.

Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Republican Senate candidate in Iowa, on Monday criticized the war in Iran for causing rising energy prices in the U.S.

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee in Michigan’s Senate race, similarly stated “Michigan families can’t afford to wait” for the Iran war to reach its conclusion, calling for an end to the conflict.

The average price of gas is $4.47 per gallon as of Tuesday, according to AAA. Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping lane for oil exports, is the primary cause of higher prices in recent months.

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told The Hill that “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party.”

articles.title: Firm tied to Trump’s social media alleges ex-partner siphoned off millions
articles.summary: The political consulting firm behind some of President Trump’s most prominent social media accounts is suing one of its co-founders, accusing him of embezzling millions to fund a lavish lifestyle and gambling addiction. X Strategies, which manages the Trump War Room and Team Trump accounts on social platform X, as well as assists with the…
articles.body:
The political consulting firm behind some of President Trump’s most prominent social media accounts is suing one of its co-founders, accusing him of embezzling millions to fund a lavish lifestyle and gambling addiction.

X Strategies, which manages the Trump War Room and Team Trump accounts on social platform X, as well as assists with the president’s TikTok, filed the complaint on Monday against co-founder Derek Utley in a South Florida federal court.

Utley founded X Strategies in 2017 at age 32 alongside then-19-year-old Alex Bruesewitz — a MAGA movement ally and influential adviser who is now behind much of Trump’s online presence.

The lawsuit, which was first reported by Politico , alleges Utley engaged in a yearslong scheme embezzling at least $5 million in company finances to fund an “extravagant lifestyle” that included purchasing luxury sports cars, designer clothing and first-class travel.

Utley, who served as X Strategies’ chairman and chief financial officer, had “exclusive access” to the firm’s bank accounts and financial records, according to the lawsuit. He also oversaw its internal operations and accounting.

The firm claims the theft began in 2021 and remained hidden in part through frequent transfers between accounts and fabricated financial records, including disguising personal purchases as business expenses. The lawsuit also alleges civil racketeering, civil theft and fraud.

“I dispute these allegations in the complaint and will address them through the legal process,” Utley said in a statement to Politico. “I have no further comment at this time.”

The lawsuit alleges Utley had an extensive gambling habit, which X Strategies’ lawyers say he funded using company money. In one year alone, the firm claims he spent 200 days at a single South Florida casino, betting tens of millions on slot machines.

X Strategies claims the older co-founder lost $3 million — winning $26 million during this period and losing $29 million. They say they were left to absorb the costs.

The reported scheme came to light after the firm hired a new president, Michael Seifert, who noticed the company’s cash on hand was much less than its reported revenues, the lawsuit states.

Around the same time, according to the complaint, the company learned Utley had called a third-party from a Las Vegas casino while “highly intoxicated” and asked for an urgent wire transfer, claiming X Strategies needed the money to make payroll the next morning.

That night, the firm alleges Utley had actually suffered a massive gambling loss and sought more money to continue betting.

The incident prompted a closer investigation and audit into the company’s finances, which uncovered “suspicious transactions” and “payments to himself,” the firm’s lawyers wrote. They also claimed that Utley initially denied taking money from the company after being confronted but later admitted to Seifert that he had stolen millions.

Utley stepped down as chairman and CFO of X Strategies in April but briefly remained as an employee. The filing states he was later fired for allegedly submitting fake medical records to secure six months of paid leave.

articles.title: Harris hits the campaign trail for El-Sayed in Michigan: Senate hopeful will be ‘a national voice’
articles.summary: Former Vice President Kamala Harris sought to boost Michigan Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed during a joint Tuesday appearance in the Great Lakes State, stressing the stakes for Michiganders in the midterms. “Remember, the Senate seat is six years. So let’s think about that in the lives of all the people that the leaders here serve,…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris sought to boost Michigan Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed during a joint Tuesday appearance in the Great Lakes State, stressing the stakes for Michiganders in the midterms.

“Remember, the Senate seat is six years. So let’s think about that in the lives of all the people that the leaders here serve, and the good work that can happen over the course of those years, because of the power and the strength of Abdul and that Senate seat,” Harris said alongside El-Sayed at a discussion on Black maternal health care.

Harris, who represented California in the Senate before she was tapped to join the Biden administration, touted her early partnership with Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.), whose retirement kicked off this year’s highly competitive Senate race.

“So I sat next to the senator from Michigan, and I have some sense then of the role that the senator, a senator from Michigan, occupies. It’s a very important one,” Harris said. “His will be a voice, Abdul’s, that is a voice representing the people of this state, and it will be a national voice.”

Her closing plea to “let’s please elect him to the United States Senate” was met with applause.

El-Sayed, a doctor and former head of health departments in Detroit and Wayne County, faces Trump-endorsed former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in a race that Cook Political Report considers a toss up and Decision Desk HQ puts under the “lean” Democratic label.

Rogers narrowly lost the 2024 Senate election to Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), even as President Trump flipped the state and defeated Harris.

Harris endorsed El-Sayed last month, saying he “understands that the power is with the people, and that the stakes couldn’t be higher in this election” as other top Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y), coalesced around the progressive.

Harris and El-Sayed spoke together on Tuesday to a roundtable of health care workers and advocates, stressing the stakes for maternal health under the Trump administration.

El-Sayed said the race against Rogers is an opportunity “to decide that we are going to invest in more health, we are going to invest in healthcare.”

articles.title: Postal worker tossed 300 mail-in ballots in a parking lot garbage out of ‘laziness’
articles.summary: Postal worker tossed 300 mail-in ballots in a parking lot garbage out of ‘laziness’
articles.body: WASHINGTON — An overwhelmed U.S. postal worker in Utah dumped 300 mail-in ballots into a parking lot garbage shortly before the state’s June 23 primary election in which both Democrats and Republicans were on the ballot, Justice Department officials said Tuesday. The 34-year-old mail carrier told investigators he did not have a political agenda, and that he also tossed other mail when he ditched the ballots, said Melissa Holyoak, U.S. attorney for the District of Utah. She said roughly 95% of voters do so by mail in the state, and it wasn’t clear yet whether they were able to eventually cast ballots. According to a government memo, Damon Matai Seei told investigators that he wanted to toss out advertisements to “lighten his workload” after feeling overwhelmed. “He claims he simply made a ‘poor decision’ out of ‘frustration’ and ‘laziness,’” the memo said. He didn’t intend to toss any ballots, they said. Seei is no longer with the U.S. Postal Service. He pleaded not guilty Tuesday to a charge of destruction and delay of mail. The Trump administration has made investigating voter fraud — which is rare — a priority, as President Donald Trump insists without evidence that noncitizens are voting en masse and has sought to limit mail-in ballots. The Supreme Court last week refused to allow the president’s mail-in restrictions to be enforced. Trump has repeatedly made false claims that he won the 2020 election and also falsely claimed he won the popular vote in 2016, yet the Trump administration has struggled during both terms to bring cases showing evidence of significant voter fraud. That’s despite a massive effort in Trump’s second term to obtain voter registration records from states in an attempt to determine if there were any noncitizens registered. So far during the president’s second term, the Justice Department has charged 70 voter-fraud related cases. At least 174 million people are registered to vote in the U.S. Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said there were more cases in the works, but he didn’t provide further details or a timeline. “Under the leadership of President Trump and Attorney General Blanche, this department is committed to protecting the vote of American citizens,” he said. The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, meanwhile is revving up a longstanding election monitoring program, but putting a new emphasis on “ballot security” and staffing the effort with newly-hired conservative personnel that have replaced longtime career employees, hundreds of whom have departed en masse since Trump came back to office. The Civil Rights Division’s efforts to seizer voter rolls has resulted in a string of court losses: with 25 courts ruling against the federal government. Voting rights experts say isolated instances of fraud do happen, as do issues with voting machines, but not on a scale that could have changed the outcome of 2020 presidential election won by Democrat Joe Biden. But the materials the Justice Department releases could help feed Trump’s broader narrative about elections. And with the majority of voters disapproving of Trump’s presidency and saying his policies have hurt the economy, Republicans are facing a tough midterms picture. Earlier this month, the Justice Department rolled out five voting-related cases, four of which were brought against non-citizens. Last week, the Justice Department announced 16 individuals had been charged in election-related cases, with a press release mentioning that at least ten of them were lawful permanent residents of the United States. The defendants were originally from Mexico, Nigeria, India, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Antigua and Barbuda, Venezuela, Columbia. There was also a defendant from Russia: Victoria Viktorivna Aquilina, a 42-year-old Russian national who entered the United States as an au pair in her early 20s, was charged with casting a ballot in the 2024 election. Trump, who until he won the 2024 election faced federal criminal charges for his efforts to overturn his 2020 loss in the lead-up to the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, said earlier this year that Republicans should “nationalize the voting.” Democrats, meanwhile, have launched an “unprecedented” effort to combat potential disruption of the 2026 election. Seei’s next court date is Nov. 30. His federal public defender did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.body:
Proposed diesel export ban splits GOP senators

Senate Republicans are clashing over a proposal endorsed by Sen. Chuck Grassley (Iowa) and other farm-state Republicans to embargo the export of diesel to increase supply and lower prices at home.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is open to the idea, but oil-state Republicans have slammed the proposal as a “gimmick.”

The soaring cost of diesel is putting political pressure on Republicans in farm states such as Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska , where Democrats now have a chance to win Senate seats that weren’t viewed as competitive a year ago.

The double whammy of President Trump’s global trade war, which has impacted commodities such as pork and soybeans, and the mounting cost of fuel and fertilizer has put farmers in a foul mood, and some Senate Republicans fear an angry backlash in key red states.

“Why doesn’t Pres Trump put an embargo on diesel exports like presidents in the 70s put embargoes on ag[riculture] products bc [because] food prices were inflated,” Grassley posted on social media over the weekend.

“High diesel prices ARE KILLING FARMERS INCOME,” he declared.

Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), who is neck and neck with her Democratic opponent Josh Turek in the polls, endorsed an embargo on diesel exports Monday and blamed Trump’s months-long war with Iran for pushing up fuel prices.

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran. We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices,” Hinson posted Monday on social platform X.

She called for suspending the gas tax, pausing diesel exports and loosening restrictions on gas with higher blends of ethanol.

articles.body:
Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) is trailing her Democratic competitor, state Rep. Josh Turek, by 8 points in the upcoming Iowa Senate race, survey results published Tuesday found.

Around 50 percent of respondents to Marists’ latest poll said they plan to vote for Turek in November, while 42 percent said the same of Hinson. Two percent said they are going to back someone else while 5 percent were unsure on their vote choice or did not answer

The survey also found that, despite Hinson polling slightly behind Turek, a majority — 59 percent — believed she would claim the Hawkeye State’s open senator position. A Democrat has not been elected to the post since 2008, and 37 percent predicted Turek would be able to flip the seat.

The fresh polling from Marist comes amid rocky political territory for the GOP, even in firmly red states like Iowa, with the Iran war driving up fuel prices, President Trump’s approval rating sagging and Republicans polling behind Democrats on issues like immigration and health care.

As of Sept. 15, nonpartisan political handicapper Cook Political Report rates the Iowa Senate race as a “toss up.”

On Monday, Hinson agreed with voters’ frustrations surrounding gas prices, saying, “Iowans shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran.”

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran. We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices,” Hinson posted on the social platform X.

The Marist poll took place from Sept. 17 to 20, featuring 1,050 Iowa registered voters and a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. The percentages included in the pollster’s report were rounded to the nearest whole number.
